name: ROS 2
summary: Connects a robot's sensors, software modules, and controllers through reusable communication tools.
why: A strong branch choice for autonomous inspection or servicing prototypes after you can write and debug small programs. Learning nodes, topics, coordinate frames, and logging helps you understand how a complete robot is organized.
firstProject: Around late 2029, after small Python and C++ programs work on Linux, publish simulated temperature readings, subscribe in a second node, and record and replay the data.
prerequisites: Working small Python programs OR basic C++ programs
Learn nodes, topics, and logging in a first project
Coordinate frames for later motion work
alternatives: Direct Python messaging for a tiny prototype
access: Free and open source; core ROS 2 uses Apache 2.0, with some packages under BSD or other licenses.
platform: Ubuntu is a practical starting point; Windows and other platform support depend on the ROS distribution and package.

sources.title: Current ROS 2 documentation and distribution guides

name: Gazebo
summary: Simulates robots, their sensors, and their interactions with a virtual physical environment.
why: Pairs naturally with ROS 2 when a rover or robot-arm project needs repeatable tests before hardware. Use it to compare a model with measurements; a convincing animation alone does not establish physical accuracy.
firstProject: Around late 2029 or later, after a simple ROS 2 project works, simulate a two-wheel indoor rover driving a short route and compare its commanded and measured travel distance.
prerequisites: Small programs in Python or C++
A simple ROS 2 publisher/subscriber if integrating with ROS 2
Basic rigid-body motion and model files
access: Free and open source; Gazebo Sim uses Apache 2.0, with dependencies under their own licenses.
platform: Ubuntu is officially supported for current Jetty releases; Windows and macOS support is best effort.

name: MoveIt 2
summary: Provides motion planning, kinematics, and collision checking for robot arms and manipulators.
why: Relevant if your equipment-cartridge project evolves into robotic insertion, inspection, or servicing. Learn it after basic robot coordinates and joint motion so that you can explain why a planned motion succeeds or fails.
firstProject: Move a simulated arm between two poses while avoiding a simple box obstacle.
alternatives: A custom planner for a simple arm
MoveIt Pro where a team licenses it
access: MoveIt 2 is free open-source software under BSD terms; the separate MoveIt Pro product has commercial licensing.
platform: Linux, especially a supported Ubuntu and ROS 2 pairing; follow the distribution compatibility table.

name: Nav2
summary: Adds navigation, route planning, obstacle handling, and recovery behaviors to ROS 2 mobile robots.
why: Useful for an indoor inspection rover once you understand basic localization and sensor limitations. Its planning and behavior components help turn a driving demo into a robot that handles repeatable tasks and reports failures.
firstProject: Navigate a simulated rover between three indoor stations and record successes, travel time, and recovery events.
access: Free and open source; follow the licenses included with the individual Nav2 packages and dependencies.
platform: Supported ROS 2 environments; the documented binary quickstart uses Ubuntu packages.

name: OpenCV
summary: Processes camera images and video for tasks such as calibration, measurement, and visual inspection.
why: A practical early addition to Python for your equipment-panel inspection idea. Start with controlled lighting, geometry, and known markers before adding machine learning; you can learn a great deal from measuring errors in a modest camera setup.
firstProject: Detect a printed marker on an equipment panel and measure how detection changes with angle and lighting.
access: Free and open source; OpenCV 4.5.0 and later use Apache 2.0.
platform: Windows, Linux, and macOS, with mobile and other platform support documented by the project.

name: PyTorch
summary: Builds and trains machine-learning models using tensors, automatic differentiation, and optional GPU acceleration.
why: Worth adding when a perception project has a real dataset and a baseline that conventional image processing cannot handle well. It is not a prerequisite for learning CAD, mechanics, controls, or basic robotics.
firstProject: Train a small classifier on your own labeled images of correctly and incorrectly assembled mock equipment, using a separate test set.
access: Free and open source under PyTorch's BSD-style license; some dependencies carry separate terms.
platform: Windows, Linux, and macOS; available GPU acceleration depends on operating system, hardware, and build.

name: NVIDIA Isaac Sim
summary: Creates detailed virtual robot environments with physics, camera simulation, and synthetic-data workflows.
why: Explore with a guided scene now if it interests you. Use it as your primary robotics simulator when a simple Python script, model, or sensor experiment gives it a clear role. Deepen coordinate frames, simulation physics, and validation through projects; no calendar year is a prerequisite.
firstProject: Place a camera and mock equipment panel in a scene, vary lighting, and compare synthetic images with real photographs.
access: Isaac Sim repository code is Apache 2.0; required Omniverse components, models, textures, and other dependencies have additional terms.
platform: Current documentation lists Windows 11 and Ubuntu with supported NVIDIA RTX hardware; check the compatibility tool and current requirements.

name: MuJoCo
summary: Simulates articulated bodies and contact for robotics research and control experiments.
why: Useful if you become interested in robot dynamics, manipulation, or learning-based control. Its compact models make repeated experiments convenient, but contact behavior still needs careful assumptions and comparison with physical observations.
firstProject: Model a simple pendulum, compare its period with a hand calculation, and study how damping changes its motion using documented assumptions and units.
access: Free and open-source code under Apache 2.0; documentation has separate Creative Commons terms.
platform: Prebuilt binaries are available for Windows, Linux, and macOS; architecture support varies.

name: PX4 Autopilot
summary: Provides an open-source autopilot stack with simulation and hardware interfaces for autonomous vehicles.
why: A branch tool for an aircraft or vehicle-controls project, rather than a requirement for spacecraft engineering. Begin in software-in-the-loop simulation to learn logs, sensors, modes, and testing without making hardware the first obstacle.
firstProject: Run a supplied virtual vehicle example and compare its logged attitude and altitude with the commanded values.
alternatives: A small custom controller for a teaching model
access: Free and open source under BSD-3-Clause; hardware and third-party components have separate costs or terms.
platform: Development on Ubuntu, macOS, or Windows through WSL 2; target and simulator support vary.

name: ArduPilot
summary: Supplies autopilot software for several vehicle types, including rovers, aircraft, and boats.
why: An alternative to PX4 if your chosen student project or hardware ecosystem already uses it. You do not need to master both stacks; vehicle simulation, logs, state estimation, and reproducible tests transfer between them.
firstProject: Use the supplied simulated rover to drive a short route and inspect its position and sensor logs.
alternatives: ROS 2 with a simple rover controller
access: Free software under GPLv3; redistribution and modification must follow those terms.
platform: Runs on supported autopilot hardware; the documented SITL workflow runs on Linux and Windows.

name: QGroundControl
summary: Provides a graphical ground station for configuring and monitoring MAVLink-compatible vehicles.
why: Useful alongside PX4 or a compatible ArduPilot project for inspecting telemetry and understanding operational workflows. It is a supporting application, not a replacement for learning the vehicle's dynamics or how its control software works.
firstProject: Connect it to a simulated vehicle and document where to inspect battery, position, attitude, and status information.
prerequisites: A supported simulator or vehicle stack
access: Free and open source; code is dual-licensed under Apache 2.0 and GPLv3-or-later, with separate artwork terms.
platform: Desktop support includes Windows, macOS, and Linux; check current releases for mobile availability.

name: F Prime (F´)
summary: Organizes embedded and spacecraft software as reusable components with commands, events, and telemetry.
why: A strong later option if you enjoy making dependable spacecraft electronics and software work together. It connects programming skills to flight-software architecture, but using a flight-proven framework does not automatically qualify your own application for spaceflight.
firstProject: Build the official Hello World example, then add a simulated temperature component and a command that changes its reporting rate.
access: Free and open source under Apache 2.0.
platform: Documented development workflows cover Linux, macOS, and Windows through WSL; embedded targets require a suitable port.

sources.title: NASA JPL F Prime overview and tutorials

name: NASA Core Flight System (cFS)
summary: Provides a reusable architecture and services for spacecraft flight-software applications.
why: Explore it when a research group, employer, or mission uses cFS; there is little reason to learn it and F Prime deeply at the same time. The public bundle is a starting point, and mission-specific verification remains essential.
firstProject: Run the public sample application on a Linux host and trace a command through to a telemetry response.
access: The public framework and listed common components are Apache 2.0; a separate government-use distribution has restricted access.
platform: The public quickstart targets a Linux host; other processors and operating systems need suitable platform support.

sources.title: NASA cFS architecture, distribution, and quickstart

name: FreeRTOS
summary: Runs small embedded applications as scheduled tasks on microcontrollers and modest processors.
why: Useful once your sensor-and-actuator project needs several activities with timing constraints. Learning tasks, queues, synchronization, and timing teaches more about dependable embedded software than immediately adding a large robotics framework.
firstProject: On a supported development board or simulator, run one task that generates temperature readings and another that logs them through a queue.
access: Free and open source under MIT terms; commercial support and separately certified variants are distinct offerings.
platform: Targets numerous microcontroller architectures; development-host support depends on the selected board and toolchain.

sources.title: FreeRTOS features, license, and supported architectures

name: Zephyr
summary: Provides a configurable embedded operating system with drivers, networking, and development tools.
why: An alternative embedded ecosystem when your board or team benefits from its driver and hardware-description support. Learn one small embedded workflow first; adopting Zephyr is most useful when it solves a concrete project need.
firstProject: Build a supported board's sensor sample, log readings, and add a simple warning state for a simulated out-of-range value.
access: Main project uses Apache 2.0; imported components can have other licenses.
platform: Host setup is documented for Ubuntu, Windows, and supported macOS systems; deployment targets supported embedded boards.

sources.title: Zephyr getting started and host platforms

name: NASA GMAT
summary: Models spacecraft orbits and mission sequences through a graphical interface, scripts, and programming interfaces.
why: A useful first dedicated mission-analysis application after gravity, vectors, and numerical integration make sense. It lets you connect a simple orbit calculation to a larger spacecraft mission study without first writing every supporting tool yourself.
firstProject: Propagate a simple Earth orbit, plot altitude over time, and compare its period with the two-body formula.
access: NASA distributes GMAT as open-source software; check the release's license and included dependency notices.
platform: NASA lists Windows, Linux, and macOS; use the distribution and setup instructions for your platform.

sources.title: NASA GMAT software catalog and operating systems

name: Ansys STK
summary: Analyzes how spacecraft, ground sites, sensors, and communications interact over time.
why: Useful for mission-level questions such as contact windows, coverage, and system trade-offs. Learn it when a course, research project, or employer needs that workflow; it overlaps with other mission tools but does not replace their underlying physics.
firstProject: Model a public satellite orbit and a ground station, then explain when line-of-sight contact is possible.
access: Commercial software; available capabilities depend on licensed products and modules. Check institutional or current student access before purchasing.
platform: STK desktop uses Windows; STK Engine also has a Linux workflow with separate requirements.

name: FreeFlyer
summary: Supports orbit analysis, spacecraft mission design, and operational flight-dynamics workflows.
why: A valuable later choice if an internship or employer uses it for mission operations. Its scripting and external interfaces support repeatable analyses; you can learn orbital fundamentals in a free tool before deciding whether this specific environment is needed.
firstProject: Create a simple satellite mission and compare predicted eclipse intervals after changing the initial orbit.
access: Commercial a.i. solutions product; request appropriate licensing or institutional access rather than assuming the name means free software.
platform: The current vendor page lists Windows, Linux, and Mac; confirm edition-specific requirements.

sources.title: FreeFlyer capabilities, licensing links, and platforms

name: Orekit
summary: Provides reusable space-dynamics calculations for orbit propagation, timing, frames, events, and estimation.
why: Useful when you want to build a custom mission-analysis application rather than operate a graphical one. It rewards careful handling of data, units, frames, and time scales, so it belongs after a basic orbital-mechanics project.
firstProject: Propagate a simple orbit and compute ground-station visibility, validating one result against an independent tool.
access: Free and open source under Apache 2.0; supporting physical-data files have their own provenance.
platform: Java-based library requiring a compatible JDK; wrapper and deployment requirements depend on the chosen environment.

sources.title: Orekit official source mirror, capabilities, and requirements

name: NASA SPICE Toolkit
summary: Calculates spacecraft and planetary geometry using mission data, reference frames, and time information.
why: Important in many planetary and spacecraft-analysis workflows when real ephemerides and consistent geometry are needed. It complements a dynamics simulator: SPICE mainly supplies geometry and data handling rather than a complete spacecraft design environment.
firstProject: Use public kernels to plot Earth–Moon distance over a month and document the time scale and reference frame.
access: Publicly available from NASA NAIF under its SPICE use rules; language wrappers may carry separate licenses.
platform: Official C toolkits include Windows, Linux, and Intel/Apple-silicon Mac variants; choose a supported compiler/platform combination.

name: Basilisk
summary: Combines spacecraft dynamics, flight algorithms, and repeatable simulation experiments in a programmable framework.
why: Especially relevant if you choose spacecraft attitude control, estimation, or integrated simulation. Its Python interface and compiled modules connect your programming foundation with serious engineering models and can later support hardware-in-the-loop testing.
firstProject: Run a documented attitude-control example, change one initial condition, and explain the resulting settling behavior with labeled time-history plots.
access: Free and open source under the ISC license; check companion-tool terms separately.
platform: Official documentation lists macOS, Linux, and Windows.

sources.title: Basilisk architecture, applications, license, and platforms

name: Tudat / TudatPy
summary: Provides programmable astrodynamics tools for propagation, estimation, and space-research studies.
why: A strong optional research path if you enjoy numerical methods and want direct control over model assumptions. Its Python interface makes it accessible from your scientific-computing foundation, while meaningful results still require orbital mechanics and validation.
firstProject: Compare two-body orbit propagation with a model including one additional perturbation, and plot the difference.
alternatives: Basilisk for spacecraft dynamics and control
access: Free and open source; TudatPy uses BSD-3-Clause with dependency licenses also applicable.
platform: Conda installation is documented for Windows, Linux, and macOS; check supported architectures and package builds.

name: MATLAB
summary: Combines a matrix-oriented programming language with numerical analysis, plotting, and engineering tools.
why: One of your core academic tools because it connects mathematics with engineering calculations and coursework. Learn arrays, functions, plots, data import, and checking numerical results; add specialized toolboxes only when a class or project needs them.
firstProject: Import a small temperature dataset, plot it with units, fit a simple model, and inspect the residual errors.
access: Commercial software with student, academic, and other licensing routes; campus access and individual toolbox entitlement must be checked.
platform: Windows, macOS, and Linux, plus MATLAB Online for supported browser workflows; feature requirements vary.

name: Simulink
summary: Models dynamic systems and controllers with block diagrams that can be simulated and tested.
why: Prioritize it when differential equations, feedback control, or a relevant course becomes part of your work. It is particularly valuable for comparing a controller with a physical-system model and understanding how changes affect stability and response.
firstProject: Simulate a room-temperature controller and compare overshoot and settling time after changing one controller parameter.
access: Commercial MathWorks product requiring appropriate MATLAB/Simulink access; code generation and specialized capabilities can require additional products.
platform: Supported MATLAB desktop platforms; confirm product, add-on, and compiler requirements for the intended workflow.

name: Simscape
summary: Models connected physical components such as motors, thermal networks, and fluid or electrical systems.
why: Useful for your equipment-bay or robotics projects when interactions between physical subsystems matter. Start with a small model whose parameters you can measure; large component libraries do not remove the need to understand conservation laws and model limits.
firstProject: Build a simple thermal mass and heat-transfer model, then compare its cooling curve with measured data.
access: Commercial add-on within the MATLAB/Simulink ecosystem; specialized Simscape products may need separate licenses.
platform: Supported MATLAB/Simulink desktop platforms; confirm requirements for each specialized add-on.

name: Stateflow
summary: Describes event-driven decisions and operating modes using state machines and graphical logic.
why: Useful when your system must switch clearly between startup, normal operation, cooling, and fault-handling modes. It complements continuous control models and makes transition conditions visible, which can help you design and test reliable behavior.
firstProject: Model an equipment monitor with off, warming, normal, and sensor-fault states, then test every transition with synthetic inputs.
alternatives: A state machine written in Python or C++
access: Commercial MathWorks product; verify Stateflow and any required simulation or code-generation entitlements.
platform: Supported MATLAB platforms; check whether the selected workflow also requires Simulink and other products.
